practice.context: A student is preparing a two-minute report about a local creek. Which plan best supports an organised presentation?
practice.correct: Introduce the topic, group two or three key facts logically, cite reliable sources for important claims, then finish with a clear concluding point.
distractors: List facts in the order they were found online.
Begin with the conclusion and omit the topic.
Use as many facts as possible without checking relevance.
practice.rationale: A structured oral report selects relevant information and organises it so the audience can follow the main point.
practice.hint: Plan a clear beginning, grouped body points and purposeful ending.

practice.context: During rehearsal, a speaker races through important information and the audience cannot follow it. What is the best adjustment?
practice.correct: Slow the pace at key information and use brief pauses to separate ideas.
distractors: Speak even faster so the talk ends sooner.
Whisper the entire presentation.
Keep the same pace but remove all punctuation from notes.
practice.rationale: Pace and pausing help listeners process important information and understand how ideas are grouped.
practice.hint: Match pace to meaning and give listeners time to process key points.

practice.context: A speaker says, “The reef is nice and has lots of stuff.” Which revision is more suitable for an informative presentation?
practice.correct: “The reef supports diverse marine species, including coral, fish and crustaceans.”
distractors: “The reef is super cool.”
“Stuff lives there.”
“The reef, like, has things.”
practice.rationale: Precise and topic-specific vocabulary communicates information clearly and appropriately.
practice.hint: Use exact words and technical vocabulary when they help the audience understand.

practice.context: A student rehearses a persuasive talk with a peer. The peer says the speaker’s voice becomes too quiet when presenting the main reason. What should the student do?
practice.correct: Rehearse that section again, increasing volume enough for the audience while keeping a natural tone.
distractors: Ignore the feedback because rehearsal should not change delivery.
Shout every sentence.
Delete the main reason.
practice.rationale: Peer feedback is useful when it identifies a specific delivery feature that can be adjusted for audience needs.
practice.hint: Use feedback to make a deliberate change to tone, pace, pitch or volume.

practice.context: A story presentation reaches a tense moment. Which delivery choice is most likely to support meaning?
practice.correct: Use a slightly slower pace and purposeful tone to emphasise the tension without exaggerating every word.
distractors: Read the whole story in exactly the same tone.
Speed through the tense moment.
Turn away from the audience and speak into the screen.
practice.rationale: Tone and pace can reinforce the meaning and mood of a story when used deliberately.
practice.hint: Choose vocal features that match the purpose of the moment.

practice.context: A presentation slide contains a detailed photograph of a nesting bird while the speaker explains where the nest is built. How should the visual be used?
practice.correct: Refer to the relevant part of the photograph while explaining it, so the visual supports rather than competes with the spoken information.
distractors: Read unrelated text while the photograph is shown.
Put as many decorative images as possible on every slide.
Assume the image explains itself and stop speaking.
practice.rationale: Visual features should add relevant information and be integrated with what the speaker says.
practice.hint: Use visuals only when they help the audience understand a specific point.

test.context: A student is preparing an argument for a safer school crossing. Which structure is strongest?
test.correct: State the position, present organised reasons supported by reliable evidence, address the audience clearly and conclude with the requested action.
distractors: Tell an unrelated story before listing random facts.
Repeat the position many times without reasons.
Show pictures without explaining the claim.
test.rationale: An oral argument needs a clear position, organised support and an audience-focused conclusion.
test.hint: Make the reasoning easy to follow from claim to evidence to requested action.

test.context: A speaker’s pitch rises and volume increases on every sentence, even neutral facts. What would improve delivery?
test.correct: Vary pitch and volume selectively so emphasis matches the meaning instead of treating every sentence as equally dramatic.
distractors: Increase volume further.
Use one very high pitch throughout.
Remove all pauses but keep the same emphasis.
test.rationale: Effective delivery uses vocal features deliberately according to purpose and audience.
test.hint: Emphasise what matters; do not emphasise everything.

test.context: Which wording best suits a short report about a solar eclipse?
test.correct: “During a solar eclipse, the Moon passes between Earth and the Sun, blocking some or all of the Sun from view.”
distractors: “The sky does a weird thing.”
“It is awesome and kind of dark.”
“Sun stuff happens behind the Moon thing.”
test.rationale: Clear, precise vocabulary helps an audience understand a technical topic accurately.
test.hint: Prefer exact nouns and verbs over vague conversational fillers.

test.context: After rehearsal, a peer says, “Your final sentence is hard to hear and your slide changes before you refer to the diagram.” Which revision best uses the feedback?
test.correct: Rehearse the final sentence at an audible volume and delay the slide change until after pointing out the relevant diagram feature.
distractors: Ignore both comments because the content is already correct.
Delete the final sentence and diagram.
Speak the whole presentation louder and advance slides faster.
test.rationale: Good rehearsal feedback identifies specific delivery and multimodal timing changes that can be practised before presenting.
test.hint: Turn specific peer feedback into a specific rehearsal action.
